title: Act II, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: A drunken Porter imagines himself porter of hell gate, joking about a farmer, an 'equivocator' and a tailor, before opening to Macduff and Lennox. Lennox describes an unruly night of storms and screams. Macduff discovers Duncan's body ('Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!'). Macbeth reveals he has killed the chamberlains, claiming fury and love; Lady Macbeth faints. Banquo vows to fight 'treasonous malice.' Malcolm and Donalbain secretly flee to England and Ireland, fearing 'daggers in men's smiles.'

context.history: The Porter's 'equivocator' is widely read as an allusion to the Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who defended misleading answers under oath.

significance: Comic relief deepens the horror: the castle has become hell's gate. Macbeth's killing of the grooms removes witnesses and makes his own guilt more visible; the princes' flight lets suspicion fall on them.
discussionQuestions: Why might a writer place a joke right after a terrible event?
Where does irony appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with ambition and its costs?

satQuestions.passage:
The night has been unruly: where we lay,
Our chimneys were blown down; and, as they say,
Lamentings heard i’ the air; strange screams of death,
And prophesying with accents terrible
Of dire combustion and confused events
New hatch’d to the woeful time: the obscure bird
Clamour’d the livelong night: some say, the earth
Was feverous and did shake.
’Twas a rough night.
My young remembrance cannot parallel
A fellow to it.
Reenter Macduff.
O horror, horror, horror! Tongue nor heart
Cannot conceive nor name thee!
What’s the matter?
Confusion now hath made his masterpiece!
Most sacrilegious murder hath broke ope
The Lord’s anointed temple, and stole thence
The life o’ the building!
What is’t you say? the life?
Mean you his majesty?
Approach the chamber, and destroy your sight
With a new Gorgon: do not bid me speak;
See, and then speak yourselves.
Exeunt Macbeth and Lennox.
Awake, awake!
Ring the alarum-bell. Murder and treason!
Banquo and Donalbain! Malcolm! awake!
Shake off this downy sleep, death’s counterfeit,
And look on death itself! up, up, and see
The great doom’s image! Malcolm! Banquo!
As from your graves rise up, and walk like sprites,
To countenance this horror! Ring the bell. Bell rings.

anchorPassages.note: “Daggers in men’s smiles”: the princes flee the near-in-blood threat.
anchorPassages.text:
What will you do? Let’s not consort with them:
To show an unfelt sorrow is an office
Which the false man does easy. I’ll to England.
To Ireland, I; our separated fortune
Shall keep us both the safer: where we are,
There’s daggers in men’s smiles: the near in blood,
The nearer bloody.
This murderous shaft that’s shot
Hath not yet lighted, and our safest way
Is to avoid the aim. Therefore, to horse;
And let us not be dainty of leave-taking,
But shift away: there’s warrant in that theft
Which steals itself, when there’s no mercy left.

segments.script: The Porter's 'equivocator' is widely read as an allusion to the Jesuit Henry Garnet, executed in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who defended misleading answers under oath. Comic relief deepens the horror: the castle has become hell's gate. Macbeth's killing of the grooms removes witnesses and makes his own guilt more visible; the princes' flight lets suspicion fall on them. Characterization: The Porter imagines himself the gatekeeper of hell, admitting an "equivocator" among others: comic relief that is also commentary. Dramatic irony: Macbeth plays the shocked host; Lady Macbeth faints (real or feigned?). Plot: Macduff discovers the body; Macbeth kills the grooms; Malcolm and Donalbain flee. Watch for kingship and order: Rightful kingship is tied to natural order; watch how disorder in the state shows up in nature.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale” slowly and put it in my own words: The drunken Porter imagines welcoming an equivocator to hell, someone who could swear on both sides of the scales. Next, craft. I notice the comic tone, which follows the murder with a joke about lying. The strongest word is “equivocator”: it means someone who speaks double meanings to deceive. Then, effect. What is the Porter joking about when he describes an equivocator? My answer: The Porter is joking about an equivocator, someone who swears to both sides and lies under oath; the joke links to the Gunpowder Plot trials and to the play's deceptive language, since the witches equivocate with Macbeth.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, dramatic irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the discovery of the murder? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act II, Scene III develops the idea of the discovery of the murder. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The Porter's comedy turns Macbeth's castle into hell. When the text says “Here’s a knocking indeed! If a man were porter of hell-gate” (Act II, Scene III, line 739), it shows this directly. He imagines himself "porter of hell-gate," admitting "an equivocator," which fits the castle where a murder has just been committed and where words will keep hiding truth.

lessonAtAGlance.objective: Students will analyze how irony develops in “Act II, Scene III” by writing a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that cites at least 2 quotations from the section, and will score at least 80% on the section quiz.

readingChunk.minutesEstimate: about 8 minutes at 150 words a minute (estimate)

anchor.opening: The night has been unruly: where we lay,
anchor.closing: To countenance this horror! Ring the bell. Bell rings.

lessonAtAGlance.assessment: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket
